title: Build vs Buy an AI Agent Platform: A Practical Evaluation Framework
excerpt: Evaluate AI agent platforms using task-level trials, operating costs, ownership boundaries, and tested exit paths before choosing what to build or buy.
content:
Choosing whether to build or buy an AI agent platform is a decision about which responsibilities your team should own. A platform can supply deployment, orchestration, evaluation, and operational interfaces. It cannot decide what a correct business outcome means or remove your responsibility for granting an agent authority.

A useful evaluation compares complete operating arrangements rather than feature checklists. This guide develops a proposed decision process and a hypothetical document-review example. The costs, thresholds, and trial results are illustrative assumptions, not vendor prices or measured benchmarks.

## Split the platform into responsibilities before comparing products

“Build” and “buy” describe a spectrum. You might write the business workflow, buy model access, use managed infrastructure, and retain your own evaluation harness. Another organization might buy a packaged application while building its authorization adapters. Treating either arrangement as purely purchased or purely internal obscures the work that remains.

Google Cloud's architecture guidance distinguishes agent runtime from model runtime and compares managed agent hosting with container and infrastructure options. Its component-level treatment is useful here: selecting a managed runtime does not automatically select every tool, memory store, or evaluation policy. This is a provider's architectural guidance, not independent evidence that one deployment option is superior. [Agent architecture components](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/choose-agentic-ai-architecture-components).

Create a responsibility map with explicit owners:

| Responsibility | Evidence needed during evaluation | Typical retained business ownership |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workflow execution | Recovery after interruption; state compatibility | Task semantics and completion criteria |
| Tool integration | Authentication, authorization, effect verification | Permission policy and business invariants |
| Evaluation | Reproducible datasets and inspectable grading | Representative cases and acceptable error types |
| Operations | Monitoring, escalation, rollback, support boundaries | Incident decisions and customer communication |
| Data lifecycle | Export, deletion, backups, migration | Information classification and retention decisions |

These are proposed evaluation categories. Their assignment depends on the actual contract and architecture. An available feature is not evidence that someone operates it for you.

## Set non-negotiable constraints before weighted preferences

A weighted score can conceal a disqualifying weakness. A system with attractive usability should not compensate numerically for an inability to enforce required tenant isolation. Separate admission requirements from preferences.

For the hypothetical review service, admission requirements might include server-enforced access to each customer's documents, an action approval that binds to a specific revision, exportable task records, and a documented procedure for disabling execution. Preferences could include a convenient visual editor or built-in dashboards.

For each requirement, define an observable demonstration. “Supports approvals” becomes: pause a proposed external action, change the underlying document, approve the old proposal, and observe that execution refuses the stale authorization. “Enterprise security” becomes a collection of specific identity, data-flow, isolation, and response requirements appropriate to your system.

NIST's AI RMF Core describes ongoing governance and management of third-party resources, along with testing before deployment and during operation. It is a voluntary risk framework, not a platform certification or a procurement checklist. A practical interpretation is that purchasing a component changes your control boundary but does not end your assessment responsibilities. [NIST AI RMF Core](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/).

## Give every candidate the same task-level trial

Vendor demonstrations usually show a favorable path through a prepared environment. Replace that with a bounded trial using representative tasks, permitted tools, and identical success criteria. Include an internal baseline, even if it is a simple application workflow rather than an autonomous agent platform.

Separate configuration effort from run performance. If one candidate requires three days of adapter development while another requires two weeks, record the difference. Then evaluate the resulting configurations on a restricted holdout set, so repeated adjustments do not turn the test into a demonstration tailored to known answers.

LangSmith's evaluation documentation distinguishes curated offline testing from production evaluation and describes benchmarking, regression testing, and backtesting. Those distinctions provide useful vocabulary for a procurement trial without requiring that particular product. Offline comparison establishes evidence for the chosen dataset; it does not establish production performance by itself. [Evaluation types](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/evaluation-types).

Require artifacts for every run: task identifier, relevant input versions, platform configuration, selected model, tool effects, acceptance result, and resource usage. Keep the evaluation dataset and grading definitions outside a candidate's exclusive control where practical. See [agent evaluation datasets](/blog/ai-agent-evaluation-datasets) for leakage and labeling considerations.

## Compare total work using an explicit model

Consider a hypothetical service processing 10,000 document-review tasks monthly. Assume a purchased platform costs 800 internal accounting units per month for its platform charge, 1,200 for model and tool usage, and 1,000 for ongoing integration and operations. Its recurring total is 3,000 units.

Assume the internal alternative costs 1,000 units for infrastructure and usage, plus 2,400 for maintenance, incident coverage, and release engineering: 3,400 units monthly. The lower infrastructure bill does not make this arrangement cheaper in total.

Now add initial work. If integration costs 4,000 units for the purchased option and construction costs 16,000 for the internal option, a twelve-month comparison is 40,000 versus 56,800 units under these assumptions. Neither result includes a migration, a major incident, or demand growth. These figures illustrate accounting structure rather than a prediction.

Normalize costs by accepted outcomes as well as submitted tasks. If 9,000 reviews meet the task criteria, divide the full relevant cost by 9,000. Include human correction work consistently in both alternatives. Do not remove failed runs from the denominator's explanation or silently price engineering time at zero.

Use sensitivity ranges for traffic, repair rates, staffing, and contract changes. A decision that reverses after a small change in one assumption deserves a reversible pilot rather than a confident long-term commitment.

## Test the exit path while access still exists

Data export is necessary but not sufficient for portability. A collection of conversation messages may omit workflow checkpoints, approval bindings, evaluator definitions, document versions, or action identities. Without those relationships, another system may be able to display history but unable to resume or investigate a task.

LangSmith documents SDK queries for runs using project, identifier, time, metadata, and other filters. This demonstrates why export evaluation should inspect the actual returned records and relationships rather than accept a generic statement that an API exists. Capabilities, quotas, retention, and contractual access must be checked against the candidate's current offering. [Query traces using the SDK](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/export-traces).

Perform a proposed exit drill with a small synthetic workload:

- Export task state, evidence references, prompts, configuration, and evaluation definitions.
- Reconstruct a completed task's decision and external effects without the original interface.
- Resume an interrupted read-only task in an alternative environment.
- Reconcile a pending mutation without assigning it a new logical action identity.
- Verify what cannot migrate, and define how those in-flight tasks will finish or be retired.

Record the migration labor and the functionality you lose. A familiar protocol or an open-source SDK can reduce some integration work without making stored state or operational behavior portable. The [MCP versus REST comparison](/blog/mcp-vs-rest-agent-tools) examines a related boundary between interface compatibility and application semantics.

## Make operational ownership contractual and testable

Ask who responds when the agent cannot finish. The platform vendor may own runtime availability while your team owns a broken tool adapter, an incorrect policy document, or an unacceptable decision. An incident can cross all four boundaries.

Write a responsibility agreement that identifies the first responder, available diagnostic evidence, escalation channel, rollback authority, and recovery owner for each failure class. Test it during the pilot. A support promise that excludes your integration path may provide little help for your most likely outage.

For an internal build, apply the same standard. Name the team maintaining dependencies, running migrations, managing credentials, and covering incidents after the original developer changes projects. Unassigned internal ownership is a dependency risk, not architectural independence.

Avoid equating self-hosting with complete control. Your deployment can still depend on a hosted model, proprietary license checks, external package registries, or an unavailable specialist. Conversely, a purchased component can be replaceable when its interfaces and data contracts are deliberately bounded.

## Make a bounded decision with an expiry condition

The decision record should state the workload, candidates, rejected alternatives, evaluation evidence, cost assumptions, retained responsibilities, and known migration gaps. Add conditions that trigger reassessment: a new authority requirement, a material workload shift, persistent quality regression, or a contract change.

For the hypothetical service, a sensible outcome might be to purchase runtime operations while retaining tool authorization and the independent evaluation harness. That is a proposed architecture under the stated assumptions, not a universal recommendation. Another team with an established platform and specialized recovery needs could reasonably reach a different decision.

Start with limited traffic and explicit rollback criteria. Expanding responsibility should depend on observed task outcomes and operational evidence. “We selected a platform” is the beginning of an ownership arrangement, not the end of engineering.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is open source always cheaper than a managed platform?

No. Evaluate licensing, hosting, maintenance, upgrades, incident response, and specialist time together. Open source may improve inspectability or flexibility, but those benefits do not make operational work disappear.

### Should a small team avoid building any agent infrastructure?

Not categorically. A narrow application can need little infrastructure beyond existing services. Compare the smallest adequate internal design with the purchased alternative, rather than assuming every internal choice requires a general-purpose platform.

### How can I reduce lock-in without building everything?

Own task definitions, evaluation cases, business permissions, and critical data contracts. Test exports and replacement paths during the pilot. Accept dependencies deliberately when their benefits justify the measured cost of leaving them.
